title: Comments of Alaskans for Data Center Accountability, et al. in opposition to the Preliminary Permit Application for the Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute and Infrastructure Hub Project under P-15423.

documents.name: 2026-11-02 NGO letter.pdf
documents.text:
BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



In the Matter of the Application of:                   )
                                                       )        Docket No. P-15423-000
DeepGreen Cook Inlet                                   )



             COMMENTS ON COOK INLET DATA CENTER
         BY ALASKANS FOR DATA CENTER ACCOUNTABILITY,
 ORGANIZATION UNDER NORTHERN ALASKA ENVIRONMENTAL CENTER;
ALASKA WILDLIFE ALLIANCE; CENTER FOR BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY; COOK
        INLETKEEPER; AND OCEAN CONSERVATION RESEARCH


       We oppose the preliminary permit application for the Cook Inlet underwater data center.

As community organizations, we urge FERC to deny DeepGreen’s application for the Cook Inlet

Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub. The proposed data center and associated preliminary

activities threaten endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales, vulnerable Pacific salmon populations,

and the unique habitat that sustains them and other wildlife.

       Alaska’s Cook Inlet should not be the testing grounds for an underwater data center. The

proposed data center in Cook Inlet, Alaska, would use up to 350 tidal turbines to power 66 server

hubs. It would be located within critical habitat for the endangered Cook Inlet beluga whale.

Data centers are known for massive energy consumption, water pollution, and heat waste.
       The proposal puts Cook Inlet beluga whales at risk. These belugas are among the most

endangered whales in the world. Only about 400 remain, and they live their entire lives in Cook

Inlet. Noise pollution from geophysical surveys and vessels can interfere with essential life

functions. Belugas depend on sound for survival, using it to communicate and hunt prey. Noise is

one of the primary threats to Cook Inlet beluga whales. Even at this early stage, the proposed

surveys and studies could disturb and displace them.

       The preliminary activities could also degrade water quality and habitat for Pacific salmon

and other native fish. Site surveys, vessel traffic, equipment deployment, and other site-
 investigation activities may disturb the seafloor and increase turbidity. These activities could

adversely affect salmon behavior and habitat. The application provides few details about the

timing or scope of the proposed activities, but those activities could further stress declining

salmon populations already facing significant pressures in Cook Inlet.

        If built, the underwater data center would be a disaster for salmon, whales, and other

wildlife. These animals are a vital part of Alaska’s identity and culture. The turbines pose risk of

entrainment, while the data center could cause noise and thermal pollution. Even the preliminary

permit activities pose risks to the health of Cook Inlet’s ecosystem. We urge FERC to prioritize

energy projects that prioritize local needs rather than an energy-intensive data center.

        FERC should recognize that this project threatens Cook Inlet’s resources. A preliminary

permit would preserve the applicant’s priority to seek a license for the proposed project. FERC

must ensure that the application is complete and determine whether the project would develop,

conserve, and use water resources in the public interest. Yet the application provides insufficient

information about the proposed activities or measures to avoid, minimize, or mitigate their

potential harm. In addition, FERC should ensure that, before any activities proceed, the applicant

obtains all necessary authorizations from the National Marine Fisheries Service to prevent harm

to wildlife and fisheries.

        For these reasons, we respectfully request that FERC deny DeepGreen’s preliminary

permit application. The application does not provide the information necessary to evaluate the

project’s environmental risks and establish that it’s in the public interest. At a minimum, FERC

should require a complete description of all proposed study and development activities, a

thorough assessment of their environmental effects, effective measures to avoid and mitigate

harm, and confirmation that all required federal authorizations will be secured before any activity

begins. Cook Inlet’s irreplaceable wildlife, fisheries, and communities should not bear the risks

of the AI data center boom.
 Dated: November 2, 2026   Sincerely,

                          Alaskans For Data Center Accountability,
                          Organization under Northern Alaska Environmental Center

                          Alaska Wildlife Alliance
                          Center for Biological Diversity

                          Cook Inletkeeper

                          Ocean Conservation Research
